gap: No result ChatGPT got gives the continuous 240 V current of the five recommended generators. Divided out, the $4,899 Honda EU7000iS gives the least at 22.9 A ($214 per amp), against 31.7 A for the Westinghouse ecoGen10000 ($41 per amp) and 37.5 A for the Champion 201417. Only the Champion and the WEN TF1050iX on gasoline or propane can sustain a 32 A load at 240 V (7,680 W).
standout_why: I compared against the two pages ChatGPT cited. The Consumer Reports inverter page lists no models, specs, amps or fuel figures in the content I could open. Lights On Labs (2026-10-27) has the EU7000iS but none of the other four; it gives 240 V only as the Honda's '30 A, 125/250 V locking outlet' and has no running amps, gallons per day or propane tanks per day. Among the uncited top results, homewelder.com gives 240 V running amps for Champion 201175, DuroMax XP11000iH and Westinghouse iGen12000DFc, but none of ChatGPT's five. rightgenerator.com's figures are tank, runtime and price only; the amps per gallon numbers in my notes were computed by me, not printed on the page.
decides: This confirms the Champion 201417 and WEN TF1050iX for a heavy 240 V load: 37.5 A and 35.6 A continuous, and both clear a 32 A EV charge or a large well pump. It weakens ChatGPT's 'premium' Honda EU7000iS pick, which gives 22.9 A at 240 V, about 61% of the Champion's 37.5 A (22.9 ÷ 37.5), at the highest cost per amp ($214). For 240 V backup the Westinghouse ecoGen10000 is still the value pick at about $41 per continuous amp, but its 7,600 W is 80 W short of a 32 A EV charge (7,680 W). On fuel per day at quarter load, the Honda is lowest at 7.65 gal, then the Champion at 9.7 gal and the ecoGen at 10.6 gal. The ecoGen figure assumes its 'up to 12 hours' is at quarter load, which its page does not say.
